There are three things I say twenty times a day, and I would put them on a sign if they let me. The first one is the question almost nobody asks. People bring me something from the shelf and they ask what it does, which is on the box, and they do not ask whether it is safe with what they already take, which is not on the box. Half the problems I catch in a week are interactions with a tablet the customer did not think to mention, because in their head that tablet is not a medicine any more, it is just something they take. The second one is the generic. It is the same active ingredient, at the same dose, and very often it costs a fraction of what the brand costs. You do not need permission and you do not need to explain yourself. You can simply ask, is there a generic, and in most cases there is. And the third one is what to do when you run out of something on a Saturday night, which is when it always happens. Do not call the clinic. Call us. In most states we can give you an emergency supply for a few days while your prescriber is unavailable, and people go the whole weekend without their medication because nobody ever told them that.

The first thing that surprised me was that almost everything was just there, on an open shelf, in an aisle, and nobody was going to hand it to me. Where I come from you ask a person behind a counter and they bring it to you. Here you walk. And the aisles have numbers and signs, and I did not know the words on the signs, so I walked past what I needed four times. The first time I collected a prescription it went badly. They told me a price and I thought that was the price of the medicine, and it seemed impossible, so I argued with a very patient young man for about ten minutes. It was the copay. The insurance was paying the rest and nobody had explained the word to me, not once, in six months of paperwork. Now I have one sentence that I use every single time, and it embarrasses me how long it took me to learn it. Excuse me, could you tell me which aisle this is in? Four words, more or less, and they solved a year of walking in circles.
